title: Goroutines: cost, scheduler and what happens in `main`

videos.script: Lesson 1 used goroutines without saying what they are. This lesson says it. {{go}} One keyword starts one. Put go in front of a call and the call runs on its own, while the code that started it carries on. Then main returns, and the program ends. The goroutine ends with it, often before it has printed a word. {{wait}} So main has to wait on purpose. A wait group does it, and the order it gives is a promise rather than luck. {{cost}} Next, the price. You start a hundred thousand goroutines and measure them. Each one begins with two kilobytes of stack. A thread asks for eight megabytes. {{sched}} Last, who runs them. The runtime has its own scheduler: goroutines, threads, and a fixed number of processors. You watch it share eight goroutines across four. And you watch it take the processor back from a loop that never lets go. {{close}} Lesson 3 gives goroutines a way to talk: the channel.
